section.title: The Time of the End
section.sectionRationale: The book closes on its highest note. Beyond the wars and the tyrants comes the greatest deliverance of all: Michael arises, God's people whose names are in the book are rescued, and the dead awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt. This is the clearest promise of resurrection in the Old Testament. Daniel is told to seal the words, to rest, and to rise at last to his inheritance, ending the book with a personal pledge of resurrection hope.
section.thesis: After the final distress, Michael stands up and God's people are delivered, the dead awake to everlasting life or everlasting contempt, the wise shine like the stars, and Daniel, though he does not fully understand, is sent on his way with the promise that he will rest and then rise to his inheritance at the end of the days.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Michael arises and the dead awake to everlasting life; seal the book until the time of the end; the sealed words that only the wise will understand; and the final promise, rest now, and rise to your inheritance.

units.label: Michael arises; the dead awake
units.note: everlasting life and the shining wise

verses.text: “At that time Michael, the great prince who stands watch over your people, will rise up. There will be a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations until that time. But at that time your people, everyone whose name is found written in the {{sepher|book}}, will be delivered.
And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will {{qits|awake}}, some to {{chayye_olam|everlasting life}}, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.
Then the {{maskilim|wise}} will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.

units.label: Seal the book until the time of the end

verses.text: But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end. Many will roam to and fro, and knowledge will increase.”
Then I, Daniel, looked and saw two others standing there, one on this bank of the river and one on the opposite bank.
One of them said to the man dressed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, “How long until the fulfillment of these wonders?”

And the man dressed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven, and I heard him swear by Him who lives forever, saying, “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time. When the power of the holy people has finally been shattered, all these things will be completed.”
I heard, but I did not understand. So I asked, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?”
“Go on your way, Daniel,” he replied, “for the words are closed up and sealed until the time of the end.
Many will be purified, made spotless, and refined, but the wicked will continue to act wickedly. None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand.
And from the time the daily sacrifice is abolished and the abomination of desolation set up, there will be 1,290 days.
Blessed is he who waits and reaches the end of the 1,335 days.

units.label: Rest, and rise to your inheritance
units.note: you will arise at the end of the days

verses.text: But as for you, go on your way until the end. You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.”

sepher.gloss: A book, scroll, written record. Deliverance belongs to everyone whose name is found written in the book, the heavenly register of God's people. The image runs through Scripture as the book of life; final salvation rests not on human strength but on being known and recorded by God.

qits.gloss: To awake, to rouse from sleep. Those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, a plain picture of bodily resurrection. This is the Old Testament's clearest promise that death is a sleep from which God will raise His people, some to everlasting life and others to judgment.

chayye_olam.gloss: Everlasting life, life of the age to come. This is the only place in the Hebrew Scriptures where the exact phrase appears; the resurrected righteous awake to chayye olam. Jesus takes up the very promise, offering everlasting life to all who believe in Him, John 5:28-29.

maskilim.gloss: The wise, those who have insight. The maskilim who suffered in chapter 11 now shine like the brightness of the heavens and like the stars forever. Their wisdom is faithfulness to God that leads many to righteousness, and it is crowned with resurrection glory.

basic.context: The final vision reaches its climax. Michael, the guardian of God's people, rises up at a time of unequaled distress, and all whose names are written in God's book are delivered. Then comes the great promise: the dead will awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame. The wise who taught righteousness will shine like stars forever. Daniel is told to seal the words until the end, is assured the wise will understand, and is sent to rest and finally to rise to his inheritance.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter gives the Old Testament's clearest teaching on bodily resurrection and final judgment, taken up directly by Jesus. The mysterious numbers and the time, times, and half a time are held with humility; the certainties are the resurrection, the two destinies, and the vindication of the faithful. The book ends not with a decoded timetable but with a personal promise of resurrection to Daniel himself.
basic.originalLanguages: Deliverance is for those written in the sepher, the book of life. The dead will qits, awake, from the dust, some to chayye olam, everlasting life, the only place this exact Hebrew phrase appears. And the maskilim, the wise, will shine like the stars forever.
basic.typology: The resurrection promised here is secured and inaugurated by Christ, the firstfruits of those who sleep. The wise who lead many to righteousness and shine like stars foreshadow all who, in Christ, turn many to righteousness and will share His glory. Daniel resting and rising points to the believer's death and resurrection in Jesus.
basic.christ: Jesus quotes this chapter, promising that all in the tombs will hear His voice and come out, some to the resurrection of life. He is the one who brings the everlasting life Daniel foresaw, having risen first Himself. The book of life is the Lamb's book, and the deliverance of God's people is accomplished by Christ, who conquered death.
basic.god: God is the living One who reigns beyond death, keeps a book of His people, and will raise the dead and judge the world. He sets the times, permits a final distress, and delivers all who are His. He refines His people through suffering and crowns the faithful with resurrection glory, so that death is not the end but a sleep before waking.
basic.crossReferences: John 5 has Jesus promising resurrection to life or judgment, echoing this chapter. First Corinthians 15 proclaims Christ the firstfruits of resurrection. And Revelation 20 shows the book of life opened at the last judgment.
basic.oneStory: The whole book has moved through empires and tyrants toward this: a final deliverance that death itself cannot stop. God's people awake to everlasting life, the wise shine like stars, and Daniel is promised his own resurrection. This hope is secured in Christ, the risen firstfruits, and it carries every believer through distress to the day they too will rise to their inheritance.

context.literary:
The chapter is the last panel of the vision that began in 10:1 and finishes the whole book. It has three movements. Verses 1 to 3 are the climax of the long speech, a short burst of three promises in the compressed style of poetry: deliverance, resurrection and shining. Verse 4 is a command to seal the book. Verses 5 to 13 form an epilogue in dialogue, in which two questions are asked and answered, "How long?" in verse 6 and "What will be the outcome?" in verse 8.

A pair of connected verbs runs through the chapter. In verse 1 Michael "stands" over the people, then "will rise up." The Hebrew uses the same verb, amad, for both. In verse 13 Daniel himself will "arise" to his inheritance, and the Hebrew is again from amad, "to stand." The one who stands guard over God's people is matched by the person who will stand in his lot at the end. The reversal is also nicely framed by 10:13, where the princes of Persia "stood against" the messenger, so that the first half of the vision is a story of opposition, and the last a story of standing to receive.

The three-part framing continues in a pattern of threes: the three promises of verses 1 to 3, the three questions or statements about time in verses 7, 11 and 12, and the three words for refining in verse 10. The time periods themselves are given in a descending scale of precision. A time, times and half a time in verse 7 is stylized, 1,290 days in verse 11 is exact, and 1,335 days in verse 12 is exact and different. The shifting numbers are a signal that the writer is not offering a simple formula.

The chapter also closes the book with a distinctive note. We have followed Daniel through lions and furnaces, kings and visions. The last verse is addressed to him personally and tells him to go his way. The man who has spent a lifetime serving empires is promised a rest and a portion that no empire can take.
context.historical:
The vision was received in 536 BC, in the third year of Cyrus, 10:1. For the people of Israel at this time, the belief in a life after death was present but undeveloped in public thought. The dead went down to Sheol, and the great hope of the nation was a restored land and a lasting dynasty. There were hints, such as Hannah's song, 1 Samuel 2:6, and the confidence of Job and some psalmists that God would not abandon them to the grave, Job 19:25 to 27 and Psalm 49:15. Isaiah 26:19 and Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones, Ezekiel 37:1 to 14, spoke of the dead living again, though the second used the image for the nation. Daniel 12:2 is the first place that speaks of the resurrection of individuals with two different outcomes.

When the persecution under Antiochus IV came in the next century, this hope became urgent. Faithful Jews were killed for refusing to break the Law, and the second book of Maccabees records that martyrs went to their deaths declaring that the king of the world would raise them to an everlasting renewal of life. That is the very promise Daniel 12 had set down.

By the time of Jesus the doctrine was divisive. The Pharisees affirmed the resurrection, and the Sadducees denied it, Acts 23:8. Martha spoke for the common view when she said her brother would rise "at the last day," John 11:24. Jesus' own teaching and the apostles' preaching assumed that Daniel 12 was true, and made it the center.

The strange numbers of 1,290 and 1,335 days belong to the same setting. A time, times and half a time had already been used in 7:25 for the period of the persecutor, and 8:14 had given 2,300 evenings and mornings for the trampling of the sanctuary. Readers under Antiochus and later readers in other persecutions have used these numbers, and the lack of agreement is itself a lesson.
context.canonical:
Daniel 12 stands at the end of a long biblical road toward resurrection. The first signs are in the stories of the dead raised by Elijah and Elisha, 1 Kings 17:17 to 24 and 2 Kings 4:32 to 37. The prophets then promise that the dead will live, Isaiah 26:19, and that God will open the graves and put His Spirit in His people, Ezekiel 37:12 to 14. Hosea speaks of being raised on the third day, Hosea 6:2. Daniel brings these hopes together and states for the first time that those who sleep in the dust will wake, some to life and some to shame.

The two destinies are tied to Isaiah 66:24, which describes the corpses of the rebels outside the city, and the Hebrew word translated "contempt" in Daniel 12:2 is the same rare word used there for the horror they will be. The book of life belongs to a tradition that begins when Moses asks to be blotted out of God's book, Exodus 32:32 to 33, and passes through the Psalms, Psalm 69:28, and Malachi 3:16 to the New Testament, where Jesus tells His disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven, Luke 10:20.

The New Testament takes up the chapter again and again. Jesus speaks of the hour when all who are in the tombs will hear His voice and come out, some to the resurrection of life and some to the resurrection of judgment, John 5:28 to 29. Paul tells Felix that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous, Acts 24:15. Jesus says that the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, Matthew 13:43, using Daniel's image. Jesus also speaks of an unparalleled distress, Matthew 24:21, using the language of Daniel 12:1. And Revelation reverses the command of verse 4, so that the angel says not to seal up the words of this book, because the time is near, Revelation 22:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The ending is meant to console people who had been told for eleven chapters about the wars and wickedness that lay ahead. It gives them a larger horizon than the history itself. The persecution is real, but it is not the end of the story, because behind the king who falls is a God who raises. The faithful who die in the persecution are not lost, and the unfaithful who prosper are not safe.

The chapter also meant to define wisdom. The wise are not the clever or the learned but those who lead many to righteousness, verse 3, and who understand when others do not, verse 10. It teaches that faithfulness in obscure times has a reward that outlasts the stars.

And it meant to teach patience. Daniel is told to seal the book and to go on his way, with no timetable he can read. The numbers are there to bound the trial, but the writer is satisfied to leave them partly unclear. He wants his readers to do what the wise do: endure, be purified, and wait for the end, with a blessing on the one who keeps waiting, verse 12.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this chapter is promise, and a promise is not a task. The resurrection will happen whether or not a person understands it. But the promise does carry commands by implication. If the dead will rise, then faithfulness at cost is worth it, as Paul argues in 1 Corinthians 15:58. If some will wake to shame, then the warning of verse 2 is to be taken seriously and not turned into an excuse for passing judgment on others, which belongs to God alone, Romans 14:10.

The closing numbers are the part most likely to be misused. They are descriptions of a coming period, given to a man who is told he will not understand them, verse 9. Treating them as a calendar, so that a modern date can be calculated, has a long history of failure, and the text itself tells readers that the matter is sealed until the end. The better use is the one verse 12 gives: to bless the one who waits.

The command to the wise is to lead many to righteousness, verse 3. That is a directive in spirit that carries forward, as in Matthew 28:19 to 20 and James 5:19 to 20.

debates.question: Who rises in verse 2, and when?

views.label: One general resurrection at the end
views.case: Verse 2 describes two outcomes from a single awakening, and Jesus speaks in the same way: all who are in the tombs will hear His voice and come out, those who did good to the resurrection of life and those who did evil to the resurrection of judgment, John 5:28 to 29. Paul tells Felix there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous, Acts 24:15. On this reading the passage is a clear statement of one final resurrection and judgment, as in Revelation 20:11 to 15.

views.label: Two resurrections, with Daniel's promise compressed
views.case: Premillennial readers note that Daniel does not say how much time separates the two groups, and that Revelation 20:4 to 6 speaks of a first resurrection of the righteous and a later one of the rest. Prophecy often draws two events together without showing the gap, as the Old Testament does with the first and second comings of Christ. Verse 2 says "many," not "all," and the word allows for a distinction in time or in group.

views.label: A resurrection of many from Israel
views.case: Some read "many" as the many of Daniel's own people, in keeping with verse 1, which speaks of 'your people.' The resurrection is then primarily that of Israel, with the wider hope of the nations made clear in later revelation. A few see a national or symbolic restoration alongside the personal one, as in Ezekiel 37.

debates.bearing: The three views agree that bodily resurrection is promised, that there are two destinies, and that the faithful are vindicated. They differ on timing and scope. The text gives no more detail, and the New Testament joins the promise to Christ's own resurrection as its first installment, 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 23, so the center of the doctrine is not in doubt.

debates.question: What are the 1,290 and 1,335 days, and the time, times and half a time?

views.label: The period of Antiochus's persecution
views.case: The three and a half years of 'a time, times and half a time' can be read as the approximate length of the desecration of the temple under Antiochus, from 167 to 164 BC. The additional thirty and seventy-five days of verses 11 and 12 would then mark the delay before the end of the crisis and the full restoration. A blessing on the one who reaches the end of the 1,335 days would be a word for those who endured to the cleansing of the temple.

views.label: A future period before the end
views.case: Others take the numbers as the length of a final tribulation, tied to the figure of Daniel 7:25 and to the three and a half years, forty-two months or 1,260 days of Revelation 11:2 to 3 and 12:6 and 14. The difference of thirty and seventy-five days is explained as an interval for judgment and the establishment of the kingdom. The verse about the abomination, 12:11, is taken as a sign, repeated in Matthew 24:15.

views.label: Symbolic of a limited time
views.case: A third group holds that the numbers are not intended to be calculated but to mark a period that is limited by God, half of seven, the number of completeness, so that the persecution is real but cut short. The varying figures are then deliberately unsettled, to discourage prediction. The repeated 'time, times and half a time' in Revelation 12:14 supports this.

debates.bearing: The writer does not explain the numbers, and the messenger tells Daniel he will not understand them, verse 9. The agreed message is that the persecution is bounded by God's oath, verse 7, and that those who wait through it are blessed. The calculation is less important than the character of the God who swore.

study.originalLanguages:
The two outcomes of verse 2 are given in a pair of unusual nouns. The first, chayye olam, is "life of the age," a phrase tied to the idea of the age to come, the life that belongs to God's coming reign. The second pair is "shame," cherpot, and "contempt," dera'on. The second is a rare word and the other place it occurs is Isaiah 66:24, where it describes the corpses of the rebels seen outside Jerusalem, and which the BSB renders as "a horror." The Hebrew in Daniel hints that the awakened wicked will be seen in the same light as that last scene of Isaiah.

The people who rise are described as "those who sleep in the dust of the earth," from the verb yashen, to sleep. Sleep is the Bible's gentle word for the death of the faithful, and the New Testament takes it up in John 11:11 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13. The pairing of "dust" and "sleep" also reverses the sentence of Genesis 3:19, that the man would return to the dust. Here the dust is the place from which people awake, just as in Isaiah 26:19, "Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust."

Verse 3 describes the wise as shining like the zohar of the sky. Zohar means brightness or radiance, and the sky is the raqia, the expanse of Genesis 1:6 to 8, a footnote in the BSB. The leaders of many to righteousness, matsdiqe harabbim, are literally those who "make many righteous." The verb is the one Isaiah 53:11 uses of the Servant, and "many," rabbim, is the same word that runs through that chapter and through Daniel 11:33. The stars are also the picture God used for Abraham's descendants, Genesis 15:5.

In verse 4 the command is to "shut up," setom, and "seal," chatom, the book. Sealing a scroll secured it and preserved it for a later reading, as in Isaiah 8:16 and Jeremiah 32:10 to 14. The text says that many will "roam to and fro," yeshotetu, and that knowledge will increase. The verb shut describes searching, as in Amos 8:12, where people run to and fro seeking the word of the LORD and do not find it, and Jeremiah 5:1, where someone is told to run about Jerusalem looking for a just man. Some scholars read "evil" for "knowledge" on the basis of the Greek text. Both readings make sense in a book that ends with searching and not finding.

The oath of verse 7 is given with both hands lifted to heaven, as in Deuteronomy 32:40, and sworn by "Him who lives forever," chai ha-olam. It is given not to promise a date but to fix a limit. The period of the "shattering of the power of the holy people" uses naphats, to smash, and the strength of the persecutor is explicitly "until" this shattering is complete.

In verse 10, three verbs describe the work of suffering: yitbarru, be cleansed, yitlabbenu, be whitened, and yitstsarefu, be refined. They mean to make pure, to make white and to smelt. The same triplet appears in the vision of Daniel 11:35. Verse 13 ends with "rest," tanuach, from the same root as Noah's name and the rest of Joshua's generation, and "lot," goral, a word used for the portion assigned by casting lots in Joshua 14:2. Daniel will stand in the portion allotted to him.

typology.fulfillment: The sentence of Genesis 3:19, "to dust you shall return," is answered by a promise that those who sleep in the dust will wake. Isaiah 26:19 and Hosea 6:2 had already hinted at it. The pattern is fulfilled in Christ, raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, 1 Corinthians 15:3 to 4, and called the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20. Matthew also notes that at His death tombs were opened and many holy ones were raised, Matthew 27:52 to 53. The type falls short because Daniel's promise concerns a future waking, while Christ's resurrection is both the guarantee and the beginning of it.

typology.type: The wise who shine like stars, Daniel 12:3
typology.fulfillment: God told Abraham that his offspring would be like the stars, Genesis 15:5, and Daniel gives that image to those who lead many to righteousness. The Servant of Isaiah 53:11 'makes many righteous,' and Jesus says the righteous will shine like the sun in His Father's kingdom, Matthew 13:43. Paul tells believers they shine as lights in the world as they hold out the word of life, Philippians 2:15 to 16. The shining of the faithful reflects the one who is the Morning Star, Revelation 22:16. The type falls short because believers shine by borrowed light, and their ability to make others righteous depends on His work, Romans 5:19.

typology.type: The book of those written, Daniel 12:1
typology.fulfillment: When Moses offers to be blotted out of God's book for the people, Exodus 32:32, he is refused as a substitute, since each answers for his own sin. The Lamb's book of life of Revelation 13:8 and 21:27 shows the answer: the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world is the one whose death secures the names written. Jesus tells the seventy to rejoice that their names are written in heaven, Luke 10:20. The type falls short because Moses could only offer himself, and God does not accept him, but Christ gives Himself and is accepted.

The land of Canaan was divided to the tribes by lot, Joshua 14:2, and the lot was an inheritance for each family. Daniel is told that he will rest, and then stand in his lot at the end of the days. The New Testament speaks of believers' inheritance as imperishable, kept in heaven, 1 Peter 1:4, and of the saints' share in the inheritance in light, Colossians 1:12. The writer of Hebrews says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9. The type falls short because Israel's lots could be lost to exile, but this inheritance is kept.

study.christ:
Jesus takes this chapter personally. When He speaks of the hour in which all who are in the tombs will hear His voice and come out, some to the resurrection of life and some to the resurrection of judgment, John 5:28 to 29, He claims for Himself the role that Daniel gave to a mysterious awakening. The voice that wakes the dead is His. He also told Martha that He is the resurrection and the life, John 11:25. The promise of a general rising that Daniel set at the end of the book is brought into the present by the One who is able to say that He gives life to whom He will, John 5:21.

The second link is that the resurrection of the Lord is the first installment of this one. Paul writes that Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, and that in Christ all will be made alive, each in his own order, 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 23. The language of "sleep" in Daniel and in Paul is the same. Because He rose, the promise to Daniel is no longer only a hope but a guarantee.

The third is the one who makes many righteous. The wise in verse 3 lead many to righteousness, and the verb recalls Isaiah 53:11, where the righteous Servant, by bearing their iniquities, makes many righteous. That is the work of Christ, and Paul says that through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous, Romans 5:19. Believers share in the calling of the wise, but only because they have first received righteousness from Him.

Fourth, the book. The names that are written in verse 1 are written in the Lamb's book, Revelation 21:27, and the sealed book of verse 4 is opened by the Lamb, who alone is worthy to break its seals, Revelation 5:1 to 9. In Revelation 22:10 the angel says not to seal up the words, because the time is near. The sealing of Daniel gives way to the opening in Christ.

Finally, Michael's rising in verse 1 should not be mistaken for the work of the Savior. Michael stands over the people as a guardian, but the one who delivers is the Lord. The New Testament describes the Lord's own descent with the voice of an archangel, 1 Thessalonians 4:16, and the one who raises is not the angel but the Lord.

The caution is that the chapter does not name Jesus and that its promise had meaning for Daniel's own readers. But the book that began with an exile ends with a resurrection, and the New Testament sees the resurrection of Christ as its fulfilment.
study.god:
The God of Daniel 12 is the one "who lives forever," verse 7. The title is given in the oath, and it is the ground of every other promise in the chapter. The empires that have filled the book are mortal, as their kings are, but the one who swears by Himself outlasts them. A God who lives forever can promise life, and He can swear that the end will come, since no tomb and no king can outlast His word.

He is the God who keeps records. A book holds the names of His people, verse 1, and a book holds all that will come, 10:21. Nothing is lost to Him. The people who feared that exile and persecution had cancelled them find that they were never absent from His notice. The same thoroughness applies to His justice: some will awake to shame, verse 2, and those who persisted in wickedness will not understand, verse 10. God's justice is not an afterthought but part of His glory.

He is also the God who is both near and not yet disclosed. Daniel is told that the words are closed until the time of the end, and yet is also told that the wise will understand. The sealing is not a sign of God's reluctance to speak but of His timing. This tension holds throughout the Bible, where some things are made known and others kept back until their time, Deuteronomy 29:29.

He refines. The verbs of verse 10 are verbs of the smith's shop: purify, whiten, refine. The suffering of God's people is neither meaningless nor the last word. God uses the heat to make something He values, and He knows how long the metal is to stay in the fire, as the oath of verse 7 sets the limit.

Last, He is gentle with Daniel. The last verse addresses the aged prophet by name, tells him to go on his way, and promises him rest and a portion. The sovereign of history takes time for one servant who did not understand. For worship, the passage teaches that the living God is to be trusted with what we do not understand, and that the right response to what is sealed is patient faithfulness.

crossReferences.note: The dead will live, their bodies will rise, and those who dwell in the dust are told to awake and sing. It is the nearest Old Testament parallel to Daniel 12:2 and shares its picture of dust and waking, as well as its joy.

God promises to open the graves of Israel and bring His people up, so that they know He is the LORD. The vision is aimed at national restoration, but its imagery of rising from graves prepares the ground for Daniel's individual promise.

The corpses of the rebels are seen outside the city, with a worm that does not die and a fire that is not quenched. The rare word translated 'contempt' in Daniel 12:2 is used here, so the two passages explain each other on the fate of the wicked.

Moses asks to be blotted out of God's book if the people are not forgiven, and the LORD says He will blot out whoever has sinned against Him. It shows that the book of Daniel 12:1 is an old idea, a register of God's people, and that membership matters.

Jesus speaks of a great distress such as has not been since the beginning of the world and says it will be cut short for the sake of the elect. His words clearly rest on Daniel 12:1 and show that He understood it as a still-unfolding pattern.

All who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of Man and come out, some to the resurrection of life and some to the resurrection of judgment. Jesus makes Daniel's promise His own and states that He is the one who calls the dead.

Paul tells Felix that he has the same hope in God as his accusers, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the unrighteous. The statement is a plain summary of Daniel 12:2 in the apostolic preaching.

Christ has been raised as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, and each will be made alive in his own order. It explains how the promise to Daniel is connected to the empty tomb: His rising is the first part of the harvest.

The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. The image is taken directly from Daniel 12:3 and applied to all believers, as an encouragement to those who live among weeds and wheat until the harvest.

An angel raises his right hand to heaven and swears by Him who lives forever that there will be no more delay and that the mystery of God will be fulfilled. It reads like a reworking of Daniel 12:7 and shows that the oath is brought to completion.

John is told not to seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, because the time is near. It is a deliberate contrast with Daniel 12:4 and 9, and marks the point at which the sealed message is opened in Christ.
Jesus tells the seventy-two not to rejoice that the spirits submit to them, but that their names are written in heaven. It takes the book of Daniel 12:1 and makes it the ground of a believer's joy.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with a sentence of death. In Genesis 3:19 the man is told that he will return to the dust, and through the whole Old Testament that sentence stands over every good thing. Kings die, prophets die, promises are held by people who are buried. The hope of the Old Testament is therefore always unfinished, since a promise made to a person who dies must find some way to outlast the grave.

Daniel 12 is the place where the Old Testament finally says it plainly. The sentence of the dust is not the last word, and those who sleep in it will wake. Earlier writers had glimpsed this in Job's confidence, Isaiah's song and Ezekiel's valley. Daniel gives it two destinies and a book of names. The theme of exile, the central trouble in Daniel, is resolved in a way the exiles could never have asked for: not return to a land but return from death.

What comes after the book is the long silence between the Testaments and then an announcement that this has begun. Jesus rises, and the apostles preach the promise as having come true in Him, Acts 4:2 and 1 Corinthians 15. The wise who lead many to righteousness become the church's witnesses, and the book that was sealed is opened. The tyrants of the age, whom Daniel saw as beasts, are shown to be doomed, and the saints receive the kingdom, Daniel 7:18 and Revelation 20:4.

The Bible ends in the new creation, where the tree of life stands again beside the river, death is no more, and the servants of God see His face, Revelation 22:1 to 5. The garden that was barred by a flaming sword is open, and the people who were once dust stand in their lot. Daniel, who was told to go on his way and rest, will stand with them. The story that began with a promise of a seed to crush the serpent ends with those who were refined and made white standing before the throne, and the book that was sealed in Babylon is read out among those who lived to see it.

quiz.q: What happens to God's people at the time of great distress?

options.text: Michael arises to stand for them, and everyone whose name is written in the book is delivered.
options.note: Daniel 12:1 promises deliverance for those written in the book.

options.text: They are all wiped out by the tyrant.
options.note: The opposite; those in the book are delivered.

options.text: They are left with no help at all.
options.note: Michael, their great prince, rises up to defend them.

options.text: They must save themselves by force.
options.note: Deliverance comes from God through Michael, not by their own force.

quiz.q: What does verse 2 teach about the dead?

options.text: Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt.
options.note: Daniel 12:2 is the Old Testament's clearest resurrection promise.

options.text: The dead simply cease to exist forever.
options.note: The verse teaches resurrection to two destinies, not annihilation for all.

options.text: Only the wicked are raised, to be judged.
options.note: Both the righteous and the wicked awake, to life or to contempt.

options.text: No one will ever rise from death.
options.note: The verse plainly promises the dead will awake.

quiz.q: What is promised to the wise who lead many to righteousness?

options.text: They will shine like the brightness of the heavens and like the stars forever and ever.
options.note: Daniel 12:3 crowns the faithful wise with shining glory.

options.text: They will be forgotten after they die.
options.note: The opposite; they shine forever, remembered and glorified.

options.text: They will rule earthly kingdoms in this life.
options.note: Their reward is everlasting shining glory, not earthly rule.

options.text: They will receive nothing special.
options.note: They are promised to shine like the stars forever.

quiz.q: How did the vision end for Daniel personally?

options.text: He was told to go his way, rest, and then rise to his inheritance at the end of the days.
options.note: Daniel 12:13 gives him a personal promise of resurrection.

options.text: He was told he would fully understand every detail at once.
options.note: He was told the words were sealed; his comfort was the promise of rising, not full understanding.

options.text: He was condemned for his many questions.
options.note: He was gently sent on his way with a promise, not condemned.

options.text: He was told there is no hope beyond death.
options.note: He was promised he would rest and rise to his inheritance.

quiz.q: How does this chapter's resurrection hope point to Christ?

options.text: Jesus quotes it, promising all in the tombs will hear His voice and rise, and He rose first as the firstfruits.
options.note: John 5:28-29 and 1 Corinthians 15 tie this hope to Christ's resurrection.

options.text: It teaches resurrection is only a symbol with no reality.
options.note: Jesus treats it as real bodily resurrection, secured in His own rising.

options.text: It predicts only Daniel would ever rise.
options.note: It promises resurrection for many, fulfilled and shared through Christ.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: Jesus directly draws on this chapter for His resurrection promise.

questions: Daniel promises the dead will awake to everlasting life. How does the certainty of resurrection change the way you face death, your own or a loved one's?
Deliverance belongs to those whose names are written in the book. What comfort do you find in resting your salvation on God's record rather than your own strength?
The wise who lead many to righteousness will shine like stars. Whom is God calling you to point toward Him, whatever it costs you now?
Daniel heard but did not fully understand, and was told to go his way in trust. Where do you need to be at peace with not understanding all of God's plan?
The book ends with rest now and rising later. How does the promise that you will rise to your inheritance steady you through present distress?

translationNotes.note: Everlasting life renders a phrase found only here in the Hebrew Scriptures; Jesus takes it up in John 5:29 for the resurrection of life and of judgment.
The wise shining like the brightness of the heavens is echoed by Jesus in Matthew 13:43, the righteous shining like the sun in the Father's kingdom.
A time, times, and half a time is the same symbolic span as in chapter 7, a limited period of distress fixed by God, sworn by the one who lives forever.
The 1,290 and 1,335 days extend the earlier figures tied to the temple's desecration; the exact reckoning is held with humility, and the blessing rests on those who faithfully wait.
